title: Unsupervised Segmentation of Fetal Brain MRI using Deep Learning Cascaded Registration
summary: This paper presents an unsupervised segmentation method for fetal brain MRI using a deep learning cascaded registration approach. The authors compare their method with existing techniques like VoxelMorph and TransMorph on the FeTa dataset, showing superior performance in terms of Dice scores.
problem_addressed: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately segmenting fetal brain MRI scans, which is crucial for diagnosing neurological conditions but can be difficult due to the variability in image quality and anatomy at different gestational stages. Previous methods like VoxelMorph and TransMorph have shown promise but this work aims to improve upon them.
method: The authors use a cascaded registration approach with an original VoxelMorph architecture, a contracted version of it, and the accumulated strategy. They evaluate these using different numbers of cascades, regularization parameters, and compare against ANTs rigid registration, VoxelMorph, TransMorph, nnU-Net, and classical MAS methods on both FeTa and IMPACT datasets.
results: The proposed method with deformation field accumulation achieves the best results, with an average Dice score of 0.866 ± 0.020 compared to VoxelMorph (0.811) and TransMorph (0.807). On the IMPACT test set, it outperforms nnU-Net for all anatomical labels, achieving a similar average Dice score of 0.926 ± 0.012.
inferences: The authors conclude that their method significantly improves segmentation accuracy in fetal brain MRI scans and is more efficient than classical MAS pipelines.
novelty_claim: The paper claims the use of an accumulated strategy with a cascaded registration approach, which outperforms existing methods like VoxelMorph and TransMorph on both FeTa and IMPACT datasets.
limitations: The authors note that the FeTa dataset is limited to four institutions and two SRR methods. The sample size for the IMPACT test set is not stated, but it includes 20 fetal brain MRI scans.
datasets: FeTa dataset [27] (160 T2-weighted fetal brain MRI scans between 20-35 gestational weeks)
IMPACT test set (20 fetal brain MRI scans)
key_findings: The proposed method with deformation field accumulation achieves an average Dice score of 0.866 ± 0.020 on the FeTa dataset, outperforming VoxelMorph and TransMorph.

title: Explainable AI for Transparent MRI Segmentation: Deep Learning and Visual Attribution in Clinical Decision Support
venue: International Journal of Computational and Experimental Science and Engineering
summary: This paper presents an explainable AI system for MRI tumor segmentation, focusing on generating visual attributions and natural language explanations to aid clinical decision-making. The authors compare their method with state-of-the-art techniques using various metrics.
problem_addressed: The paper addresses the need for transparency in deep learning models used in medical imaging by proposing a method that not only segments tumors accurately but also provides interpretable visual attributions and natural language explanations, which are currently lacking in many existing approaches.
method: The authors use a deep learning model to segment MRI images of brain tumors. They generate visual attributions using techniques like Grad-CAM to highlight important regions for the segmentation decision. Additionally, they produce natural language explanations that describe why certain areas were segmented as tumor or non-tumor. The method is evaluated on the BraTS dataset and compared against state-of-the-art methods.
results: The proposed method achieved competitive performance with state-of-the-art techniques in terms of segmentation accuracy. Natural language explanations generated by the model received high scores (BLEU, ROUGE) when compared to human-generated explanations. Visual attributions were found to be effective in highlighting relevant regions for tumor segmentation.
inferences: The authors conclude that their method provides a transparent and interpretable approach to MRI tumor segmentation, which can aid clinicians in making informed decisions. The combination of visual attributions and natural language explanations enhances the usability of deep learning models in clinical settings.
novelty_claim: The paper claims to introduce an explainable AI system for MRI tumor segmentation that combines accurate segmentation with interpretable visual attributions and natural language explanations, addressing a gap in current state-of-the-art methods.
limitations: The authors note that the dataset used (BraTS) is limited in size and may not fully generalize to all clinical scenarios. Additionally, while the method provides explanations, it does not explicitly validate whether these explanations are always accurate or aligned with human understanding of tumor segmentation.
metrics: BLEU and ROUGE scores for natural language explanations
key_findings: The proposed method achieved competitive segmentation accuracy while providing interpretable visual attributions and natural language explanations, enhancing the transparency of deep learning models in clinical decision support.

title: UM-CAM: Uncertainty-weighted Multi-resolution Class Activation Maps for Weakly-supervised Fetal Brain Segmentation
venue: International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention
summary: The paper introduces UM-CAM, an uncertainty-weighted multi-resolution class activation map method for weakly-supervised fetal brain segmentation, achieving superior performance compared to other weakly-supervised methods and a fully supervised baseline.
problem_addressed: Previous weakly-supervised semantic segmentation approaches like Grad-CAM++, Score-CAM, Ablation-CAM, AMR, and DRS struggled with accurate boundary delineation in fetal brain images. The paper aims to address this limitation by proposing UM-CAM, which incorporates uncertainty weighting for improved segmentation quality.
method: UM-CAM uses a multi-resolution approach combined with uncertainty weighting to generate class activation maps for weakly-supervised fetal brain segmentation. It compares its performance against several existing methods including Grad-CAM++, Score-CAM, Ablation-CAM, AMR, and DRS on the testing set.
results: UM-CAM achieved an average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 90.22% and an average Hausdorff Distance at 95th percentile (HD95) of 4.04 pixels, outperforming other weakly-supervised methods by at least 3.02 pixels in HD95.
inferences: The authors conclude that UM-CAM's superior performance indicates its effectiveness in generating more accurate boundary segments for fetal brain images compared to existing weakly-supervised approaches.
novelty_claim: UM-CAM introduces an uncertainty-weighted multi-resolution class activation map method, which significantly improves the accuracy of weakly-supervised fetal brain segmentation.
limitations: The paper does not explicitly discuss any limitations but given that it uses a single dataset and compares against existing methods without additional controls or validation, there may be concerns about generalizability to other datasets or clinical scenarios.
datasets: Testing set for comparison with other weakly-supervised methods
key_findings: UM-CAM achieved state-of-the-art performance in weakly-supervised fetal brain segmentation, with an average DSC of 90.22% and HD95 of 4.04 pixels.

title: Automated Brain Tumor Segmentation and Classification in MRI Using YOLO-Based Deep Learning
summary: This paper evaluates the performance of YOLO-based deep learning models in automated brain tumor segmentation and classification using MRI data, comparing them with established methods like RCNN, Faster RCNN, and Mask RCNN. The results show that YOLOv7 outperforms other models in terms of box detection accuracy and mask segmentation accuracy.
problem_addressed: The paper addresses the need for accurate and efficient brain tumor segmentation and classification in MRI images, which is crucial for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. Previous methods like RCNN, Faster RCNN, and Mask RCNN have been used but may not offer the same level of performance as YOLO-based models.
method: The authors use a dataset consisting of 827 labeled box and mask images to evaluate the precision and recall performance of YOLOv5 and YOLOv7. The evaluation metrics include mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU thresholds of 0.5, 0.5-0.95, and for specific tumor types such as meningioma and glioma.
results: YOLOv7 achieved higher box detection accuracy (0.936) and mask segmentation accuracy (0.935) compared to other models. The mAP scores were also higher at both IoU thresholds of 0.5 and 0.5-0.95, with YOLOv7 showing the highest performance for meningioma.
inferences: The authors conclude that YOLO-based models offer superior performance in brain tumor segmentation and classification tasks, making them a promising tool for clinical applications. They argue that these models can improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce the time required for manual segmentation.
novelty_claim: The paper claims that YOLOv7 outperforms other established methods like RCNN, Faster RCNN, and Mask RCNN in terms of box detection and mask segmentation accuracy for brain tumor classification tasks.
limitations: The sample size is relatively small with only 827 labeled images. The generalizability of the results may be limited to specific types of tumors or MRI scans. There are no explicit controls for other factors that could influence performance, such as image quality or preprocessing steps.
datasets: A dataset consisting of 827 labeled box and mask images
metrics: Mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU threshold of 0.5
Mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU threshold of 0.5-0.95
key_findings: YOLOv7 achieved higher box detection and mask segmentation accuracy compared to other models, making it a promising tool for brain tumor segmentation and classification in MRI images.

title: Towards Reliable and Reproducible Fetal Brain Biometry: A Deep Learning Approach Using MRI
summary: This paper presents a deep learning approach for fetal brain biometry using MRI, comparing its performance against an existing method by Luis et al. [3]. The authors evaluate their model on several biometric measurements and find that it generally outperforms the competitor in terms of error metrics, except for certain specific measurements where the competitor shows better accuracy.
problem_addressed: The paper addresses the need for more accurate and reliable methods in fetal brain biometry to support quantitative assessment of brain development. Previous methods had limitations in accuracy, particularly for specific measurements like LCC and sBIP.
method: The authors developed a deep learning pipeline for predicting fetal brain biometric measurements from MRI scans. They compared their method against an existing approach by Luis et al. [3] using statistical measures such as mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE), and Pearson correlation coefficient (R).
results: The authors' deep learning pipeline generally yielded lower error metrics across most biometric measurements, with significant improvements in sBIP and LCC compared to the competitor method. However, there were no significant differences for other measurements like HV, bBIP, and TCD.
inferences: The authors conclude that their deep learning approach is more accurate than the existing method by Luis et al., especially for certain specific biometric measurements, but overall performance was only slightly better in most cases.
novelty_claim: The paper claims to present a new deep learning pipeline for fetal brain biometry using MRI scans, which outperforms an existing approach by Luis et al. [3] in terms of accuracy and reliability.
limitations: The authors note that the sample size is not stated, limiting generalizability. Additionally, while their method shows improvements in some measurements, it does not significantly outperform the competitor in most cases, suggesting potential limitations in overall performance.
datasets: MRI scans of fetal brains used for training and testing the deep learning pipeline
key_findings: The proposed deep learning approach achieved significant improvements in sBIP and LCC measurements compared to the existing method by Luis et al., but overall performance was only slightly better for most biometric measurements.

title: A Deep Attentive Convolutional Neural Network for Automatic Cortical Plate Segmentation in Fetal MRI
summary: This paper presents a deep attentive fully convolutional neural network for automatic segmentation of the cortical plate in fetal MRI, comparing its performance against other methods using Dice, 95HD, and ASD metrics, and demonstrating superior accuracy and speed.
problem_addressed: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately segmenting the cortical plate (CP) in fetal MRI images, which is crucial for diagnosing various conditions but can be difficult due to low image quality and motion artifacts. Previous methods like multi-atlas segmentation (MAS) are slower and less accurate in lower-quality reconstructions.
method: The proposed model uses a backbone fully convolutional encoder-decoder network with forward skip connections and an attention reﬁnement module, trained on sliding, overlapping 3D patches of size 64 × 64 × 64. The model was evaluated using Dice, 95HD, and ASD metrics, comparing it to other methods like 3D U-Net, PAUNet, Attention U-Net, SE-FCN, and DSRNet.
results: The proposed method outperformed other models in terms of Dice, 95HD, and ASD metrics. It also generated CP segmentations faster than MAS, which took about 20 minutes compared to less than a minute for the proposed model.
inferences: The authors conclude that their deep supervision strategy improves segmentation accuracy and robustness, making it suitable for use in low-quality reconstructions where other methods fail.
novelty_claim: The paper claims the novelty lies in its deep attentive fully convolutional neural network architecture with stagewise forward skip connections and attention reﬁnement module, which outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and speed.
limitations: The sample size for testing is not stated. The method assumes access to high-quality training data, which may limit generalizability. The evaluation was based on a small number of test subjects (15), and the results might vary with larger or different populations.
datasets: Training and test data from fetal MRI images
key_findings: The proposed deep attentive fully convolutional neural network outperformed existing methods in segmenting the cortical plate of fetal MRI images, achieving higher accuracy and faster computation times.

title: Segmentation of the cortical plate in fetal brain MRI with a topological loss
summary: This paper presents a topological loss function for improving segmentation of the cortical plate in fetal brain MRI, comparing it to a baseline U-Net model on 35 GA atlas patches. The topological method shows improvements in Dice score, average surface distance, Hausdorff distance, and Betti error.
problem_addressed: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately segmenting the cortical plate in fetal brain MRI, which is difficult due to high computational costs associated with persistent homology and the need for improved segmentation performance over existing methods like U-Net.
method: The authors use a topological loss function (TopoCP) on 64x64 patches of T2-weighted images. Data augmentation includes random flipping and rotation by multiples of 90 degrees. The method is compared to a baseline U-Net model using quantitative metrics such as Dice score, average surface distance, Hausdorff distance, and Betti error.
results: TopoCP outperformed the baseline U-Net in all evaluated metrics: Dice score (0.70±0.14 vs 0.54±0.16), average surface distance (1.41±1.64 mm vs 2.51±2.34 mm), Hausdorff distance (5.31±5.20 mm vs 7.32±6.57 mm), and Betti error (0.68±1.27 vs 0.74±1.3).
inferences: The authors conclude that the topological loss function improves segmentation accuracy, particularly in detecting deep sulci and midsagittal areas.
novelty_claim: The paper claims a novel approach using a topological loss function to improve the accuracy of fetal brain MRI segmentation compared to existing methods like U-Net.
limitations: The sample size is limited to 35 GA atlas patches, which may limit generalizability. The study does not address long-term or clinical outcomes and only evaluates performance on static images.
datasets: 35 GA atlas patches from T2-weighted MRI
key_findings: The topological loss function (TopoCP) significantly improved segmentation accuracy over the baseline U-Net model in all evaluated metrics.

title: Prenatal serotonin reuptake inhibitor exposure and maternal depression symptoms are associated with altered fetal brain and placental development
summary: This study investigated the impact of prenatal exposure to serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SRIs) and maternal depression on fetal brain and placental development using MRI. The research involved a cohort of subjects, though specific numbers are not provided.
problem_addressed: The study aimed to address gaps in understanding how SRIs and maternal depression during pregnancy affect fetal development by utilizing advanced imaging techniques such as T2-weighted MRI and diffusion weighted imaging (DWI).
method: The study used MRI scans of the placenta at various gestational weeks, with analyses controlling for factors like gestational age, sex, maternal weight, and maternal depression scores. Least squares means from analysis of covariance were reported to evaluate differences between SRI-exposed and unexposed groups.
results: Results showed consistent findings in sensitivity analyses excluding participants with alcohol use during pregnancy, indicating that the main placenta measures (Table 3) were robust. However, specific effect sizes or p-values are not provided in the given text.
inferences: The authors suggest that their findings support a link between SRI exposure and altered placental development, but caution that maternal depression may also play a role due to unmeasured factors like physical activity and fetal movement patterns.
novelty_claim: The study claims to provide new insights into the impact of SRIs on fetal brain and placental development using advanced imaging techniques in a cohort of pregnant women with SRI exposure.
limitations: Limitations include the lack of detailed data on SRI exposure timing, duration, and amount; potential confounding factors such as maternal depression and unmeasured physiological processes; and possible underrepresentation of milder depressive symptoms due to exclusion criteria.
datasets: diffusion weighted imaging scans with different b values
Results of least squares means from analysis of covariance, controlling for gestational age at MRI scan, sex, maternal weight at MRI, and maternal depression score
Placenta measures in SRI-exposed group vs unexposed controls
key_findings: The study found consistent evidence that prenatal SRI exposure is associated with altered placental development, though maternal depression may also influence these outcomes.

title: Evaluating Synthetic Data Generation for Domain Generalization in Fetal Brain MRI Segmentation
summary: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of synthetic data generation techniques (FetalSynthSeg and RealSynthHybrid) compared to real fetal brain MRI segmentation models (FetalRealSeg and BOUNTI) in domain generalization for fetal brain MRI segmentation tasks, using FeTA 2024 training data. The results show that while FetalRealSeg and RealSynthHybrid perform slightly better on datasets close to the training distribution, synthetic methods are competitive or superior when tested on more diverse datasets.
problem_addressed: The paper addresses the challenge of domain generalization in fetal brain MRI segmentation models trained on a specific dataset (FeTA 2024), where variations in acquisition protocols and imaging conditions can affect model performance. The key limitation is that existing methods may not generalize well to unseen data due to distributional shifts.
method: The authors retrain FetalSynthSeg, FetalRealSeg, and RealSynthHybrid on the full FeTA 2024 training set (n=120) and evaluate them against BOUNTI and nnU-Net models. The evaluation is conducted across multiple testing splits from the dHCP dataset and a subset of FeTA 2024 test data, covering different MRI modalities and field strengths.
results: Table 2 shows that FetalRealSeg and RealSynthHybrid outperform FetalSynthSeg on datasets close to the training distribution. However, in more diverse testing conditions, synthetic methods are competitive or superior, as evidenced by their performance surpassing existing SoTA models like BOUNTI and nnU-Net.
inferences: The authors conclude that while real data is beneficial for domain-specific tasks, synthetic data generation can be a viable alternative to achieve better generalization across different imaging conditions. This suggests that synthetic data could potentially reduce the need for large, diverse training datasets.
novelty_claim: The paper claims to demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data in achieving domain generalization for fetal brain MRI segmentation tasks, which is not typically addressed by existing methods focused on specific acquisition protocols or pathologies.
limitations: The sample size for testing (348 subjects) may limit generalizability. The evaluation does not include a direct comparison with models trained on the same FeTA 2024 dataset but using different training strategies, which could provide additional insights into model robustness.
metrics: Wilcoxon rank-sum test for statistical significance
key_findings: Real and hybrid synthetic models outperform purely synthetic ones on datasets similar to the training distribution, but synthetic methods are competitive or superior in more diverse testing conditions.

title: ResNet-34 with Lightweight Decoder for Accurate and Efficient Segmentation of Fetal Brain MRI
summary: This paper presents a ResNet-34 with a lightweight decoder for accurate and efficient segmentation of fetal brain MRI, comparing its performance against baseline and state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and computational complexity.
problem_addressed: The paper addresses the need for both high accuracy and low computational cost in fetal brain MRI segmentation models, which is crucial for clinical applications where speed and precision are paramount.
method: The authors propose a ResNet-34 architecture with a lightweight decoder. They evaluate this model against baseline architectures using various metrics, including performance and computational complexity. The study includes an ablation analysis to assess the impact of CLAHE preprocessing and contrast-stratified performance evaluation.
results: Table 4.2 shows that the proposed model outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy while maintaining lower computational complexity compared to some baseline models (Table 4.3). Table 4.4 indicates that CLAHE preprocessing significantly improves the model's performance, and Table 4.5 demonstrates consistent performance across different contrast levels.
inferences: The authors conclude that their proposed model offers a balanced solution for accurate and efficient fetal brain MRI segmentation, suitable for clinical use due to its high accuracy and low computational requirements.
novelty_claim: The paper claims the novelty lies in achieving both high accuracy and lower computational complexity compared to existing models through the use of ResNet-34 with a lightweight decoder architecture.
limitations: The authors note that their study is limited by the specific dataset used, which may not fully generalize to all MRI imaging conditions. Additionally, the evaluation was conducted on a single type of MRI contrast, potentially limiting the model's performance in diverse clinical scenarios.
datasets: A self-collected dataset of fetal brain MRI images
key_findings: The proposed ResNet-34 with lightweight decoder achieved higher accuracy and lower computational complexity compared to state-of-the-art methods in fetal brain MRI segmentation.

title: Annotation-free deep learning for detection and segmentation of fetal germinal matrix-intraventricular hemorrhage in brain MRI
summary: This paper presents an annotation-free deep learning approach for detecting and segmenting fetal germinal matrix-intraventricular hemorrhage (GM-IVH) in brain MRI scans. The model was trained on a dataset of 100 annotated GM-IVH cases, achieving high AUROC and AUPR scores during internal validation.
problem_addressed: Prior work required extensive manual annotation for detecting GM-IVH, which is time-consuming and resource-intensive. This paper aims to address this by developing an automated method that can detect and segment GM-IVH without the need for manual annotations.
method: The authors used a deep learning model trained on 100 annotated cases of GM-IVH from brain MRI scans. The model was then validated internally using another set of 50 annotated cases, achieving high AUROC and AUPR scores. Additionally, a reader study was conducted to evaluate the performance of the model compared to human readers.
results: The internal validation achieved an AUROC of 0.928, an AUPR of 0.884, and a sensitivity at fixed specificity of 0.559. The external validation set also showed promising results with an AUROC of 0.930.
inferences: The authors conclude that their annotation-free deep learning approach can achieve high performance in detecting and segmenting GM-IVH, potentially reducing the need for extensive manual annotations.
novelty_claim: The paper claims to present a novel annotation-free deep learning method for detecting and segmenting GM-IVH in brain MRI scans, which could significantly reduce the time and resources required for manual annotation.
limitations: The authors note that the model's performance may be limited by the size of the training dataset. Additionally, the reader study was conducted with a small number of participants, limiting generalizability.
datasets: 100 annotated GM-IVH cases used for internal training and validation
key_findings: The proposed annotation-free deep learning model achieved high AUROC and AUPR scores in detecting and segmenting GM-IVH, demonstrating its potential for reducing the need for manual annotations.

title: A survey of MRI-based brain tissue segmentation using deep learning
summary: This paper surveys deep learning-based methods for MRI brain tissue segmentation across different age groups (normal adults, fetuses, and infants) using various public datasets. It introduces an ExSwin Transformer module designed to capture long-range dependencies and reports high Dice scores on the FeTA 2021 dataset.
problem_addressed: The paper addresses the lack of comprehensive surveys focusing specifically on deep learning methods for brain tissue segmentation in different age groups, particularly fetuses and infants, where limited public datasets exist.
method: The authors reviewed existing literature to compile a summary of state-of-the-art methods using various public and challenge datasets. They introduced an ExSwin Transformer module designed to enhance long-range dependency capture in deep learning models for brain tissue segmentation.
inferences: The introduction of the ExSwin Transformer module achieved high Dice scores on the FeTA 2021 dataset, suggesting its effectiveness in improving segmentation accuracy. The survey highlights the predominance of U-Net structures in fetal brain tissue segmentation models.
novelty_claim: The paper introduces an ExSwin Transformer module designed to capture long-range dependencies and correlations between different samples for deep learning-based brain tissue segmentation.
limitations: The limitations include the absence of concrete outcomes reported, reliance on existing datasets without new contributions, and the focus on summarizing rather than presenting original experimental results.
key_findings: The ExSwin Transformer module achieved high Dice scores on the FeTA 2021 dataset, demonstrating its potential for improving deep learning-based brain tissue segmentation.
